blogs.title: Observing Re-entry Break-ups
blogs.description: The amount of dedicated observation campaigns to study re-entry break-up events, be it via on-ground, on-orbit, or in-situ sensors, is surprisingly low given that on average an object with mass above one ton re-enters the Earth’s atmosphere every two weeks. Here we browse through the available literature.

history.htmlContent:
Between the first space launch on October 4, 1957 and January 2016, more than 41 500 metric tons worth of man-made objects have been placed in orbit around the Earth, the Sun, or other planetary bodies by 5197 launch events. During the same period, more than 23600 man-made objects are confirmed to have re-entered into the Earth's atmosphere, amounting to approximately 33200 metric tons. In terms of numbers, the majority of these objects are space debris (43%), e.g. fragmentation remnants or delaminated parts of intact spacecraft, followed by mission related objects (32%), e.g. lens covers or kick stages separated from spacecraft, and intact spacecraft such as satellites and rocket bodies (25%). In terms of mass, the vast majority of this is associated with human spaceflight activities, e.g. the 135 Shuttle flights alone cover about 13 300 metric tons, followed by spend rocket bodies and satellites, also called payloads, in the same order of magnitude. Re-entries can intuitively be categories into two categories: Controlled re-entries, where the spacecraft actively determines the time and location of the entry point into the atmosphere, and uncontrolled re-entries, where either the time or the location can no longer be influenced by the spacecraft and has to be described stochastically.

Controlled re-entries tend to target remote regions of the Earth's surface to avoid damage to property and humans on-ground, or to enable easy identification of the spacecraft after re-entry in case of human spaceflight missions and interplanetary return capsules. As such they tend to have only minimal risk potential. Uncontrolled re-entries on the other hand are left to the natural forces to guide their decay from orbit, and for this class it is instructive to look into the historical trends in more depth. The frequency of payloads and rocket bodies re-entering over the last decades follows a similar trend. On average one can say that in the current decade we have seen the re-entry of an intact spacecraft on a weekly basis, leading to between 50 and 100 metric tons re-entering yearly. The recent spike in the number of re-entering payloads during the last three years is attributed to CubeSat and other small spacecraft, which have been launched by about a 100 per year in mainly short-lived orbits. They do not significantly contribute to the total yearly re-entering mass. The higher frequency and mass during the seventies and eighties is a relic of the high launch traffic to low Earth orbits during the cold war. These numbers are still dwarfed in comparison to the Earth atmospheric entry of natural objects, i.e. meteoroids, which amount to about 40 000 metric tons per year, they are most likely in the sub-millimetre regime. The re-entry of meteorites with a diameter of 1 metre or larger are rare, at about once a year, whereas for spacecraft this is about every other week during the last decade.

Confirmed re-entry events since the beginning of the space age

Count (left) and mass (right) of payloads associated to re-entry events since the beginning of the space age

Count (left) and mass (right) of rocket bodies associated to re-entry events since the beginning of the space age

modelling.htmlContent:
Re-entry predictions in general come down to the capacity of long- (years), mid- (a few weeks), and short-term (less than a day) orbit propagations and the ability to forecast the accompanying input parameters to the environment models. The first major perturbation factor for the orbit propagation is the non-spherical Earth, which as an enacted force that can be expressed by the harmonic expansion of a gravity potential field. For re-entry predictions models with orders well below a 100 are generally sufficient, depending on the orbits under consideration. The same type of harmonic expansions can be made for the gravity potential fields of the Sun and Moon, which can have a strong impact on the re-entry predictions for orbits with a high eccentricity. However here an order of one is already sufficient for the vast majority of cases.

A second major perturbation from the re-entry predictions point of view is due to the motion of the satellite through and atmosphere. This perturbation depends on the local atmospheric density, the aerodynamic velocity with respect to the atmosphere (accounting for the Earth rotation and winds), the ratio of the projected cross-section in direction of the aerodynamic velocity to the mass, and the aerodynamic coefficients of the spacecraft. For most orbital applications, including re-entry predictions, the aerodynamic coefficients are reduced to a drag and lift term which capture the resistance (drag) and generated lift of an object in a fluid. The later one is usually assumed to be 0, apart for analysis or re-entry vehicles in the lower layers of the atmosphere.

The first major difficulty in predicting re-entries is due to the dependency on knowing the local atmospheric density along the trajectory of the orbit. This density for an equilibrium state is defined by the energy input, coming from the Sun under the form of extreme ultraviolet radiation and particle streams in the solar wind, and energy dissipation, by internal processes such as Joule heating, ionisation, or chemical reactions, for each of the individual atoms and molecules making up the atmosphere, i.e. mainly N2, N, O, O2, Ar, He, and H. The solution of these equilibrium equations are dependent on the geodetic latitude, longitude, altitude. Solving the equilibrium equation, i.e. the coupled (perfect) gas equation, hydrostatic equation under the gravity field, and the diffusive thermal equilibrium equation, is one issue, but accurately modelling the input for the Sun is another one. In reality, only proxies can be used to mimic the energy input. Often used proxies for this are the solar radio flux at 10.7 cm (2800 MHz), indicator of disturbances in the Earth's magnetic field as captured in the planetary K-index, or simply the Sun spot number which underlies both. These proxies are selected for our ability to measure them on Earth, not necessarily because they correlated best to the atmospheric physics. Moreover, they are notoriously difficult to forecast reliably for more than a few days.

Next to difficulties in forecasting the local atmospheric density also the ballistic coefficient is not trivial to use in practical predictions. Foremost the project cross-section for a non-convex spacecraft can vary strongly with the view angle, i.e. under the assumption of different attitude motions. This can lead to huge variations in the ballistic coefficient. Similarly, the mass is difficult to estimate in practice, e.g. due to uncertainties on the propellant on-board a spacecraft. The drag coefficient depends on the shape, material, the speed-ratio, the temperature, and the flow regime. The flow field can be capture by three main numbers:

  • The Mach number, which is the ration of the local flow velocity to the speed of sound of the medium. This captures the ratio of kinetic energy to internal energy of the flow. Hypersonic velocities are generally considered to have Mach number 5 or above, but are shape and material dependent.
  • The Reynolds number, which is the ratio of the product of the local density with local flow velocity with the object's reference length to the dynamic viscosity term of the medium. This captures the ratio of pressure forces to viscous forces. Low Reynolds number flow as called laminar, leading to smooth motion of the medium. High Reynolds number are called turbulent, characterised by instabilities in the flow.
  • The Knudsen number, which is the ratio of the mean free path length to the characteristic length of the object. This captures the interaction of the particles of the flow with the object. Flows with Knudsen numbers above 10 are generally considered as within the free molecular regime, Knudsen numbers below 0.01 as the continuum flow regime, with the transition or rarefied regime in between.

As the ballistic coefficient is difficult to derive for any given object and moreover variable, e.g. it can be done in the frame of precise orbit determination for navigation or scientific satellites, alternatively it is often estimated as part of space surveillance processes. The ballistic coefficient is often a by-product from orbit determination procedure to fit the observed orbit decay during the data gathering period. Without directly using observations but when ephemeris are available instead, the ballistic coefficient can be estimated by using a time series of semi-major axis values:

  1. The initial estimate for is obtained by back-propagating the final state of the window to match the first state;
  2. And iterate on to minimise the residuals for all the intermediate values of the semi-major axis in the time series.

Once an object reaches the atmospheric entry point, a commonly understood interface where the orbital velocity starts to decrease due to the interaction with the atmosphere, a three degrees of freedom, or even six degrees of freedom, analysis as in the previous section is no longer sufficient to capture all the physics acting on the object. Concretely, the aerodynamic deceleration and aerothermal heating need to be modelled to understand the final part of the re-entry trajectory and the structural impact on the object. In a rough approximation, the re-entry interface point for a spacecraft on a circular orbit is around 120 km in altitude above the Earth. Note that in general the Knudsen number starts to drop at an altitude between 100 and 150 km. Half an orbit later, the spacecraft will be between 100 and 90 km of altitude above the Earth, where the density of the atmosphere is high enough to rip of parts of the spacecraft with weak structural connections, e.g. MLI foil or solar arrays. A few minutes later, between 75 and 80 km of altitude above the Earth, observational evidence suggest that object undergoes a thermal break-up of the main structure. Multiple break-up fragments released this way will travel on average another 7 minutes before reaching the Earth's surface, if at all. During this time, they reach peak heating between 45 and 65 km of altitude above the Earth, and peak deceleration between 35 and 55 km of altitude above the Earth. The extend of the impacts between fragments along a hypothetical ground-track of an intact spacecraft, i.e. the so called footprint, can be many hundreds or kilometres long.

Not all fragmentation events are thermal induced, but residual fuel or build up pressure in the spacecraft can lead to an explosive break-up when coming in contact with the atmosphere. Such case have, for example, been extensively studied for ESA's Automated Transfer Vehicle. The probability to trigger and explosion will in general dependent on the type of combustion agents, the effective temperature reached by the spacecraft, and the local pressure. The general effect of an explosion, altitude dependent, will be to stretch the footprint of the re-entry potentially up to a few thousands of kilometres.

Analytical approximations for the aerothermodynamical processes, i.e. heating, during the re-entry are available for spheres, cylinders, boxes, or flat plates, which can serve as theoretical input to assess the survivability of an object, but in general more complex solvers are required. There are currently three categories of computational frameworks in existence which deal with the aerothermal processes encountered by re-entering objects:

  • Full CFD codes which numerical solve the Navier-Stokes equations to analyse the flow equations around arbitrary bodies and can be combined with chemistry models to compute surface interactions between objects and flow. These codes have extensively been used for, among others, the design of atmospheric entry vehicles to survive the re-entry, and to predict and understand observations made in wind tunnel experiments across all accessible flow regimes.
  • Spacecraft-oriented models, which represent a spacecraft's atmospheric entry in a full finite element based 6 degrees of freedom simulation under simplified aerothermal dynamics. These models aim to provide a first order physical approximation to the re-entry behaviour of a spacecraft and rely on verification against CFD codes and experiments to justify their predictive functionality. They can be used as on-ground casualty risk validation software.
  • Object-oriented tools, which represent a spacecraft's atmospheric entry as simplified translational, or with constrained rotation, trajectory alone with aerothermal dynamics derived from theoretical simplifications of the relevant equations. These tools enable parametric investigations and aim at the validation of on-ground casualty risk requirement under well-defined, often conservative, conditions. The verification of these models is often based on Spacecraft-oriented models.
These frameworks have a clear function during the design of a spacecraft. In case of an object designed to survive the re-entry, CDF codes are indispensable to guaranty the intended flight and ablation behaviour of an object. When starting on the design of a general satellite or launcher, object oriented tools can be used to do a first break-up assessment and are easy to iteration on when the design changes. In case the break-up fragments are unlikely to pose a risk on ground, this approach can be followed until launch. If a risk is however found, spacecraft-oriented models can be used during the building and reviewing phase of spacecraft development, to investigate if the surviving fragments are due to model simplification or if real measures in the design are required to counter the risk.

observations.htmlContent:
The thermal and mechanical processes which drive the break-up of a spacecraft when re-entering the Earth's atmosphere produce enough heating to be observable from ground, including during daytime in certain cases. On top of those processes, an explosion of the spacecraft can occur when sufficient amount of propellant is still on the spacecraft when it re-enters. Over the past few decades, a number of in-situ observation campaigns have been undertaken to gain a better understanding of the physics involved in re-entry break-ups. Initially these observations focused on the tracking of the fragments produced, later on these type of measurements were complemented by a host of observations in different wavelength down to full spectroscopy.

A thermo mechanical break-up will cause a so called 'string of pearls' to be observable, where fragments with higher ballistic coefficients are follow by fragments with lower ballistic coefficients on a re-entry trajectory are visible due to the radiation given off by heating. When most of the velocity is removed from the fragments due to friction with the atmosphere, surviving fragments fall down under the influence of gravity creating a footprint from a few 100km up to a 1000km in length of potential impact points. In case of an explosive re-entry, a significant cross-track component is added to the footprint. Below, examples of visual observations from ESA's Automated Transfer Vehicles 1 and 4 are respectively made by tracking cameras on ground and from the International Space Station.

recoveredDebris.htmlContent:
When spacecraft re-enter into the Earth's atmosphere, most of it will break up due to aerothermal and mechanical loads and burn up due to the heat. Nonetheless there are cases, when fragments of spacecraft or space debris survive the re-entry and impact on ground. This website provides a list of recovered space debris, if possible giving detailed information about mass, geometry, material, discovery location, source part and possible origin, from reputable sources. The data is gathered from several scientific papers, conference documents, government documents, and news outlets. There is no claim to completeness of this data. Corrections, missing information, or enquiries for more details can be sent to Preentry_support@esa.int (remove the capital P).

In broad terms, all regions of the Earth are affected by re-entries as can be seen above, where the predicted re-entry location is given for all the satellites and launcher stages which re-entered prior to November 2016 from a circular orbit. The abundance of re-entries all over the globe is in sharp contrast with the location of fragments on ground which could be identified as re-entry debris. Next to the individual locations, four major events can be marked: Cosmos 954 in Canada in 1978, Skylab in 1979 in Australia, Salyut 7 in 1991 over Argentina and the Columbia accident 2003 in the United States of America, which all resulted in a larger number of fragments found on ground by dedicated searches. These events are marked as the light-blue dots in the figure.

Key Facts on Recovered Debris

Since the beginning of space age, the following fact have been gathered on presumed uncontrolled re-entries of space debris objects:

  • In total about 80 impact zones around the world have been more than tentatively associated with re-entries
  • 166 debris objects recovered over 55 years - about four metric tons - excluding the four major events with dedicated searches
  • Particularly abundant: pressure vessels - 73 cases

However, an posterior analysis is not always conclusive and the implication of a source object can be tentative at best. In the list below, we will only report on objects found on ground which have strong or proven correlation with an object which was in orbit. This reduced the amount of impact zones to 67, the recovered fragments to 150, out of which 58 are pressure vessels.

Typical examples for recovered debris fragments are displayed in the figure above. The picture on the left shows a typical pressure vessel for rocket bodies. This one was recovered in 1963 in Australia. More recent examples for pressure vessels were recovered in Brazil, Spain and Indonesia during the last years. Nowadays they are built as composite overwrapped pressure vessels (COPV) and act usually as pressure tanks, e.g. for helium. The last picture shows typical ablation markings on recovered pieces of debris.

The most often, against the statistical odds, identified parent object of re-entry debris is a Delta rocket second stage, from which several tanks were recovered, weighting about 250 kg each. They also represent the largest objects as seen in the figure below. Next to the Delta rocket debris, there are some typical cases for the more modern pressure vessels, which are recovered all over the world. There have been only three cases when space debris has directly hit someone's property, however no humans or animals were harmed. In one case a woman got struck by a piece of lightweight material which has been tentatively identified as space debris, but also in this case there was no injury.

Next to re-entry events where at most one to six objects were found by 'coincidence', there have been several re-entries and break-ups of bigger spacecraft where dedicated searches were undertaken to find debris pieces. The most known might be the tragic accident of Space Shuttle Columbia after mission STS-107, when the shuttle disintegrated due to aerothermal superheating and melting of the wing structure. A piece of foam damaged the thermal shield during the launch. In a large recovery operation about 84000 fragments were found, covering about 38% of the shuttle's dry mass. Also important was the re-entry of the space station Skylab which re-entered in a semi-controlled way in 1979 over the Indian Ocean and South-West-Australia. More than 30 pieces of debris (all sizes and shapes) can be seen in a museum in Esperance, out of the more than 500 recovered. Another major re-entry event was the one of Cosmos 954, a nuclear fission reactor powered RORSAT satellite which re-entered in winter 1978 over the remote parts of North-West-Canada. About 4000 tiny radiating flares next to several beryllium rods were spread over a large area of about 130000 km2.

workshop.htmlContent:
The atmospheric re-entry of return capsules and manned space objects has been under continuous study since the beginning of the space age. Nowadays also the monitoring of the re-entry of space debris objects and the prediction of re-entry break-up processes has become part of nominal operations and mission design.

The first international workshop on re-entry of space debris was organised by ESA in 1983 in response to the re-entries of Skylab and Cosmos-1402, and has been repeated over the past decades in response to other significant re-entry events. Since then the topic has broadened from individual re-entries to include, among other, full object catalogue predictions, orbital lifetime assessment, and thermo-mechanical fragmentation in the lower atmosphere. From the point of view of space debris, the entire orbital lifetime after the end of mission down to potential impact on ground needs to be addressed.

The intended audience for these workshops are academia, spacecraft, launcher, and space surveillance operators, space agencies, and industry. Participation is free of charge. The proceedings of the past five workshops are available here by selecting the corresponding names from the 'Conference name' list.

6th Space Debris Re-entry Workshop (2025)

We are pleased to announce the 6th International Space-Debris Re-Entry Workshop, which will take place on January 15, 2025 at the European Space Operations Centre (ESOC) Press Centre. This workshop continues the tradition of fostering collaboration and data exchange within the space debris and re-entry community.

This year’s event is designed to provide hands-on, workshop-style environment with a focus on collaboration rather than a formal symposium. During the workshop, ESA will release and make available new data from the re-entry events of the last two years:

  • the assisted re-entry of Aeolus (July 2023),
  • the natural re-entry of ERS-2 after manoeuvres to lower its orbit (February 2024),
  • the uncontrolled re-entry of OPS-SAT, which kept running experiments to the end (May 2024),
  • the targeted re-entry of Cluster-2, where orbital changes were made to change the target region of its uncontrolled re-entry, observed from an airplane (September 2024).

These recent-re-entries have provided a lot of data, and the workshop will explore how this information can be used to improve re-entry modelling and predictability, drawing lessons from these cases to refine future approaches. There will be three working sessions:

  1. Science of re-entry: focusing on re-entry physics, material demisability and atmospheric interaction, with specific data-driven insights from the above missions,
  2. Modelling challenges: addressing the challenges in re-entry break-up modelling tools to accurately predict re-entry trajectories and outcomes, and how the latest data can help resolve them,
  3. Observation campaigns: discussing coordinated observation efforts to further improve data collection from both ground- and space-based sensors, and even air-based sensors.

While this is not a symposium and abstracts are not required, feel free to contact us if you’re interested in presenting any of these topics.

Please notice that attendance on-site is subject to capacity limits. Registered participants will be informed if such measures apply. Participation in the workshop is free of charge.

We look forward to welcoming you to this workshop!

More information on the workshop can be found at https://indico.esa.int/event/549/.

5th Space Debris Re-entry Workshop (2020; Virtual)

The 5th International Space Debris Re-entry Workshop took place 2 December 2020 fully virtually.

This workshop addressed the side effects of the increased traffic to orbit which triggered a renewed interest in the practicalities of having objects, large and small, re-entering uncontrolled after the end of their mission. The symposium style for the past events made place for a workshop around the open problems burgeoning by the increase in uncontrolled re-entry "traffic":

  1. The non-uniform distribution of the Earth gravity field and atmospheric density, combined with the forecast of space weather indices, imply multi-modal distributions on reaching the re-entry interface which differ when the timescale goes from hours up to years. Various techniques in uncertainty propagation, including aspects of space surveillance and space weather, are under development or have been explored, but need to be benchmarked and cross-compared to see how they suit the use cases. Issues are further exemplified when moving from 3 degrees of freedom to 6 degrees. How to transition from uncertainty assessment to operational products when it comes to re-entry predictions and orbital lifetimes?
  2. Once the re-entry interface is reached, a strong driver in the risk associated to re-entry events is the first fragmentation of the object within the transition regime between free molecular and continuum aerothermodynamics. Early stage research on thermal and mechanical demise physics imply large differences in predicted secondary fragmentation and the heat seen by components, with a strong need for experiments and observations identified. Which multi-physics driven break-up processes produce predictions which can be verified on a macroscopic level to cause first fragmentation?

The conference program is available here.

4th Space Debris Re-entry Workshop (2018)

The last iteration of the Space Debris Re-entry Workshop was organised on the 28th of February and 1st of March 2018 at the premises of the European Space Operations Centre (ESA/ESOC), Darmstadt, Germany. The workshop started at 14h on 28th of February and ran until 12h the 1st of March. Of particular interest for this iteration was the motion and break-up of large and heavy artificial objects in the lower thermosphere. In general, contributions were sought on the following topics (non-exhaustive):

  • Orbital lifetime estimation
  • Re-entry prediction uncertainties
  • Re-entry predictions on catalogue level
  • Low thermosphere orbit observations and orbit determination
  • Attitude-Orbit coupling effects on re-entries
  • Atmospheric break-up: physics, observations, and modelling
  • Material and aerothermal responses to changing flow conditions
  • Ground impact analysis

The abstract submission has been closed on 2nd of February 2018. Registration was possible until the 23rd of February 2018.

The conference program is available here.
